name: Wisdom & Stories
tagline: Reflections, experiences, and philosophical insights from chemists worldwide.
seo_title: Wisdom & Stories — the human side of chemistry | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Wisdom & Stories on LinkedIn and Facebook: stories, reflections and lessons from chemists past and present.

definition.lead: Wisdom & Stories shares the human side of chemistry: the doubt, persistence, luck and insight behind discoveries, told through chemists past and present.
definition.body: Papers report results; stories explain how people got there. Seeing how others handled failure, rivalry, mentorship and ethical choices helps every scientist do better work, and stay motivated while doing it.

facts.label: Nobel Prizes won by Marie Curie, in physics and in chemistry
Mendeleev's periodic table grew out of writing a textbook for his students

branches.name: Persistence
branches.summary: Years of work behind a single result.
branches.example: Marie Curie processed tonnes of pitchblende residue to isolate radium.

branches.name: Serendipity
branches.summary: Noticing the unexpected, and asking why.
branches.example: Perkin's failed quinine synthesis gave the first synthetic dye.

branches.name: Mentorship
branches.summary: How great scientists are formed by other scientists.
branches.example: Michael Faraday began as Humphry Davy's assistant.

branches.name: Ethics & responsibility
branches.summary: Science can help or harm; scientists choose.
branches.example: Fritz Haber's legacy: fertilizer for billions, and chemical weapons.

branches.name: Collaboration & credit
branches.summary: Who did the work, and who gets remembered.
branches.example: Rosalind Franklin's essential role in the DNA structure.

branches.name: Failure & resilience
branches.summary: Ideas that were rejected before they were celebrated.
branches.example: Dan Shechtman's quasicrystals were ridiculed, then won a Nobel Prize.

branches.name: Curiosity
branches.summary: Science done for the joy of finding out.
branches.example: Agnes Pockels measured surface films in her kitchen.

branches.name: Careers & choices
branches.summary: The paths chemists take, and why.
branches.example: From the lab bench to industry, policy and teaching.

timeline.title: An apprentice joins Davy
timeline.text: Michael Faraday, a bookbinder's apprentice with little schooling, becomes Humphry Davy's assistant.
timeline.why: He became one of the greatest experimental scientists.

timeline.title: The prepared mind
timeline.text: Louis Pasteur tells his audience in Lille that chance favours only the prepared mind.
timeline.why: Still the best summary of how discoveries happen.

timeline.title: An 18-year-old's failure
timeline.text: William Perkin fails to make quinine and finds mauveine instead.
timeline.why: He built an industry from a failed experiment.

timeline.title: A kitchen laboratory
timeline.text: Agnes Pockels, with no university access, publishes surface measurements in Nature with Lord Rayleigh's help.
timeline.why: Talent can come from outside institutions.

timeline.title: Radium isolated
timeline.text: Marie and Pierre Curie, working in a shed, isolate a radium compound.
timeline.why: Years of hard physical work behind one result.

timeline.title: A divisive Nobel Prize
timeline.text: Fritz Haber's prize for ammonia synthesis draws protest over his role in chemical warfare.
timeline.why: Science and ethics cannot be separated.

timeline.title: Photo 51
timeline.text: Rosalind Franklin's team records the X-ray image that reveals DNA's helical structure.

timeline.title: An 'impossible' crystal
timeline.text: Dan Shechtman observes a diffraction pattern that most experts said could not exist.
timeline.why: He was mocked for years before the Nobel Prize in 2011.

quiz.q: Who said that chance favours only the prepared mind?
quiz.explain: In an 1854 lecture at the University of Lille.

quiz.q: How did Michael Faraday start his scientific career?
quiz.explain: He had trained as a bookbinder and attended Davy's public lectures.

quiz.q: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in…
How were Dan Shechtman's quasicrystals first received?
options: They were ridiculed, then won the 2011 Nobel Prize
quiz.explain: Linus Pauling was among the most prominent critics.

quiz.q: Who recorded 'Photo 51', the X-ray image of DNA?
options: Rosalind Franklin's team, with Raymond Gosling
quiz.explain: It was shown to Watson without her knowledge.

quiz.q: How old was William Perkin when he discovered mauveine?
quiz.explain: He was working in a home laboratory during the Easter holiday.

quiz.q: Where did Agnes Pockels do her surface experiments?
quiz.explain: Women could not attend German universities at the time.

quiz.q: Why is Fritz Haber's legacy debated?
options: His ammonia synthesis feeds billions, but he also led chemical weapons work in World War I
He never won a Nobel Prize for his work
His results on ammonia were later shown to be faked
He discovered nothing that is still used today
quiz.explain: A lasting example of the ethical weight of science.

quiz.q: Mendeleev's periodic table grew out of…
quiz.explain: He needed a logical way to present the elements.

quiz.q: Why share failures, not only successes?
options: Others learn from them and avoid repeating them

quiz.q: How did Marie Curie obtain radium?
options: By processing tonnes of pitchblende residue largely by hand
By finding pure radium in a mine
By making it in a reactor
quiz.explain: The work took years in a poorly equipped shed.

quiz.q: Who helped Agnes Pockels publish her work in Nature?
quiz.explain: She wrote to him; he forwarded her letter to the journal.

labels.map_sub: The themes that come back again and again in the lives of chemists.
